title: Platform Buyers SLA scripting and procurement playbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a field-ready playbook for PLG -> sales handoff to platform/infra buyers evaluating reserved inference capacity. Focus: short, procurement-safe messaging that emphasizes predictable throughput, workload isolation, and contractual SLAs without overselling technical details. Use in discovery calls, procurement email threads, and legal negotiations.

Audience / buyer personas:
- Platform Architect (primary): cares about isolation, tenant risk, capacity planning and integration effort.
- SRE / Reliability Lead: cares about latency p99/p95, failover, tracing and runbook behaviors.
- Procurement / Legal: cares about guarantee language, exit clauses, penalties, monitoring evidence.
- Finance / CTO: TCO, commitment terms, flexibility to scale or ramp down.

Core value statements to lead with (one-liners):
- "Predictable per-tenant throughput with isolation guarantees so your product SLAs don’t hinge on noisy neighbors."
- "Dedicated GPU pools with SLA-backed latency and availability, and migration paths to private deployments when needed."
- "Contractual routing and fallback policies ensure service continuity during regional or capacity events."

Top 6 messages mapped to buyer needs:
- Predictability (Finance, Platform): fixed throughput floors, committed SKU mapping, demonstrable cost/unit with example bill scenarios.
- Isolation (Security, Platform): logical and physical tenancy options, data plane separation, KMS integration for keys.
- Measurability (SRE, Legal): token-level metering, audit logs, and monthly compliance report for throughput and uptime.
- SLA specifics (Procurement): uptime window, latency SLOs for p95/p99, credits calculation mechanics.
- Operational handover (Eng lead): runbook, playbooks, on-call handoff and escalation contacts.
- Flexibility (CTO/Finance): burst capacity, scale-up windows, and limited-term lookback to reclassify reserved commit.

Short procurement-ready SLA language (plain English snippets you can paste into an RFP response):
- Uptime: "Redwood Inference will provide 99.95% availability for the Dedicated Inference Endpoint on a monthly basis, measured as the percentage of successful request responses within configured timeouts."
- Latency SLO: "For provisioned clusters, p95 inference latency will not exceed X ms for baseline model variant under sustained load up to the committed throughput."
- Credits: "If Redwood fails to meet the uptime or latency commitments in a calendar month, the Customer will be eligible for service credits equal to a percentage of monthly committed fees as defined in the schedule."
- Isolation assurance: "Customer workloads are hosted on isolated GPU pools. Redwood will not co-locate production inference workloads from other customers on reserved hardware for the term of the commitment unless explicitly agreed."

NOTE: replace X ms with benchmarked number from the performance profile for the specific SKU/model pair before sending to procurement.

Competitive angle (how to frame vs cloud-managed endpoints and DIY infra):
- Against managed cloud provider endpoints: emphasize predictable per-token economics under sustained load and isolation as a product feature (cloud endpoints may oversubscribe hardware and surface variable performance).
- Against self-hosted inference frameworks: emphasize OPEX simplicity, integrated rollout/fallback tooling, and audit trail for compliance. DIY often hides ops burden and non-linear headcount costs.
- Against other inference vendors: call out our combined tranche: runtime optimizations + routing policies + turnkey private deployment options — not just a model serving layer.

Objections & rebuttals (sales scripts):
- "We can get cheaper GPUs ourselves." -> "Upfront cost is part of the picture. Our reserved SKU includes ongoing optimization, continuous batching, and reduced tokens/unit from caching — that often reduces effective unit cost versus DIY once you factor ops and reliability headcount."
- "We need full air-gapped on-prem for compliance." -> "We offer private deployments and a VPC-friendly control plane; let's surface the compliance checklist and schedule an architecture review with Solutions Engineering to validate gap closure."
- "How do we trust the SLA numbers?" -> "We publish verified model performance profiles. We’ll commit to a benchmarked profile for your primary model and include a measuring hook you can read directly (token-level metrics and traces)."

Procurement checklist (quick yes/no table to accelerate RFP responses):
- Committed throughput SKU defined and mapped to model family? -> Yes/No (provide SKU id).
- Measurable latency p95/p99 for selected model under committed load? -> Yes/No (attach benchmark).
- Isolation level (logical/physical) requested? -> Logical / Physical / Both.
- KMS/HSM integration required? -> Yes/No (provide key type).
- Data residency/region constraints? -> List regions.
- Exit/termination: runbook for model export and cache purge? -> Describe.

Negotiation tactics for commercial teams:
- Anchor on committed throughput first, then offer optional burst pools rather than flexible scale as the primary concession. This preserves predictability while meeting buyer desire for elasticity.
- Offer an initial 6- to 12-month pilot at a smaller commit level with the option to roll into a larger annual reservation with a defined price ladder.
- Carve out an SLA uplift (tighter latency p95) as a paid add-on instead of discounting base fees.

Field play examples (short vignettes to copy into playbooks):
1) Enterprise search company: platform lead worried about spikes from background indexing. Messaging: "Map indexing workloads to a non-production burst pool and commit user-facing inference to a reserved pool with strict isolation. We'll instrument and show delta in p99 tail latency after migration."
2) Healthcare payer: procurement insists on audit trail & KMS. Messaging: "We’ll provision a private control plane in your VPC, enable KMS integration, and produce weekly audit exports during onboarding to prove data controls."

Appendix: evidence & follow-up assets to attach in sales kits:
- Model performance profiles (per SKU/model): attach as Excel or CSV.
- Sample SLA schedule with credit calculation formula.
- Runbook checklist (incident detection -> communication -> remediation -> postmortem).
- Reference contacts for customers using reserved capacity (ask Solutions Eng for three matches).

Open questions / items for product/legal sync (items to finalize before finalizing RFP):
- Exact credit percentages and cap on credits for combined uptime+latency misses.
- Standard wording for permitted co-location (if any) and migration windows.
- Metrics export format and retention window for audit logs.

Next steps (owner: Asha Banerjee):
- Sync with Solutions Engineering to generate 3 sample benchmark profiles for the most common enterprise model families (2/26).
- Draft formal SLA schedule for legal review with credit ladder options (3/3).
- Create one-pager templates (sales) and a procurement-ready email template (3/7).

Sample procurement-ready email (copyable):
"Hi [Procurement],
Per our discussion, attached is the draft Schedule outlining Reserved Inference SKU, committed throughput, and the proposed SLA. The schedule includes measurable latency p95 targets, isolation guarantees, and the service credit ladder. Please review the benchmarked performance profile we ran against your primary model and let us know which sections you want to discuss next week.
Best,
Asha Banerjee
Redwood Inference"

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep SLA language modular so we can swap in model-specific numbers without redoing legal redlines.
- Offer measurable proofs early in procurement cycles — they defuse performance skepticism quickly.
- Don’t promise absolute isolation if a customer wants lower price; surface tradeoffs explicitly.

End of playbook.
